summary: A revision of RFC 1310 that defines the official procedures for creating and documenting Internet Standards. It is informational. It was replaced by RFC 2026.

plainLanguage.summary: This document explains how a protocol becomes an Internet Standard. It names the bodies involved and lists the levels a document passes through on its way from a proposal to a standard. It also sets out the review and waiting periods each step requires, and says how to appeal when someone disagrees with a decision.

questions: what are the standards track maturity levels
how does an internet draft become a standard
how do you appeal an iesg decision
subtitle: The rules by which the IETF turns a working group document into an Internet Standard.

tldr.problem: The Internet depends on protocols that work across networks run by many independent organizations, so somebody has to decide what counts as a standard, who decides, and how a disputed decision is challenged.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out the organizations involved, the maturity levels a document passes through, the review and approval steps for each standards action, and the appeal path when a decision is contested.
tldr.outcome: The process is designed to be open and fair while still requiring prior implementation and testing. RFC 1602 was obsoleted by RFC 2026.

sections.title: What an Internet Standard Is
sections.content:
The Internet supports host-to-host communication through voluntary adherence to open protocols and procedures defined by Internet Standards. There are also many isolated internets, sets of interconnected networks that are not connected to the Internet but use the same standards.

In general, an Internet Standard is a specification that is stable and well understood, is technically competent, has multiple, independent and interoperable implementations with substantial operational experience, enjoys significant public support, and is recognizably useful in some or all parts of the Internet. The process described in the document is concerned with all protocols, procedures and conventions used in or by the Internet, whether or not they are part of the TCP/IP protocol suite.

The procedures are designed to be fair, open and objective, to reflect existing proven practice, and to be flexible. They give all interested parties ample opportunity to participate and comment: at each stage a specification is repeatedly discussed and its merits debated in open meetings and public electronic mailing lists, and it is made available for review through worldwide online directories. They aim to recognize generally accepted practices, so a candidate specification is implemented and tested for correct operation and interoperability by multiple independent parties, and used in increasingly demanding environments, before it can be adopted as an Internet Standard.

The stated goals are technical excellence, prior implementation and testing, clear, short and easily understandable documentation, openness and fairness, and timeliness. The document notes that technical competence, prior testing and the need to let everyone comment all take time, while the pace of networking technology calls for timely standards, and that the rules are meant to balance those conflicting goals.
sections.plainLanguage: An Internet Standard is not just a good document. It has to be stable, understood, implemented by several independent groups that work with each other, used in real networks for a while, and useful. The process is built so that anyone can take part and comment, and it insists on real implementations before a specification can become a standard.

sections.title: The Organizations Involved
sections.content:
The IETF is a loosely self-organized group of people who make technical contributions to the engineering and evolution of the Internet. It is the principal body engaged in developing new Internet Standard specifications, although it is not itself part of the Internet Society. The IETF is composed of individual Working Groups, which are grouped into Areas, each coordinated by one or more Area Directors. Nominations to the Internet Architecture Board and the Internet Engineering Steering Group are made by a nominating committee selected at random from regular IETF meeting attendees who have volunteered to serve.

Internet standardization is an organized activity of the Internet Society, a professional society concerned with the growth and evolution of the worldwide Internet. Its Board of Trustees approves appointments to the IAB from among the nominees submitted by the nominating committee.

The IESG, the Internet Engineering Steering Group, is responsible for the technical management of IETF activities and the Internet Standards process. As part of the Internet Society it administers that process according to the rules in this document, and is directly responsible for entry into and movement along the standards track, including final approval of specifications as Internet Standards. It is composed of the IETF Area Directors and the chairperson of the IETF, who also chairs the IESG.

The IAB, the Internet Architecture Board, is a technical advisory group of the Internet Society, chartered by its Trustees to provide oversight of the architecture of the Internet and its protocols, and to serve as the body to which decisions of the IESG may be appealed. It approves appointments to the IESG from among the nominees submitted by the nominating committee.

The IRTF, the Internet Research Task Force, is not directly part of the standards process. It investigates topics too uncertain, too advanced or insufficiently well understood to be the subject of standardization; when an IRTF activity produces a specification stable enough to consider, that specification is processed through the IETF using the rules in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Four groups share the work. Working groups inside the IETF write the specifications. The IESG, made up of area directors, decides whether a document moves up the ladder. The IAB watches the architecture and hears appeals against IESG decisions. The Internet Society's trustees appoint the IAB and approve the process itself. The IRTF does research and hands anything stable enough to the IETF.

sections.title: Maturity and Requirement Levels
sections.content:
Documents on the standards track pass through stages of development, testing and acceptance, formally labelled maturity levels. Proposed Standard is the entry level: the specification is generally stable, its design choices are resolved, it has received significant community review and appears valuable, though further experience might still change or even retract it. Implementors should treat Proposed Standards as immature specifications, and deploying implementations into a disruption-sensitive customer base is not normally advisable. The IESG may require implementation or operational experience before granting this status to a specification that materially affects the core Internet protocols.

Draft Standard is a major advance: at least two independent and interoperable implementations have been developed and sufficient successful operational experience has been obtained. It must be well understood and quite stable, both in its semantics and as a basis for an implementation, though it may still need more field experience. Internet Standard is reached when significant implementation and successful operational experience have been obtained, and is characterised by a high degree of technical maturity and a generally held belief that the protocol or service provides significant benefit to the Internet community. A Draft Standard is normally considered a final specification, and it is reasonable for vendors to deploy implementations of Draft Standards.

Specifications not on the standards track carry one of four off-track levels: Prototype, Experimental, Informational and Historic. Prototype is similar to Experimental except that it indicates the protocol is specifically being developed to become a standard. Experimental typically denotes a specification that is part of some research or development effort. Informational is published for general information and does not represent an Internet community consensus or recommendation. Historic is assigned to a specification that has been superseded by a more recent one or is otherwise obsolete.

An Applicability Statement may also apply a requirement level to each specification it refers to: Required, Recommended and Elective for standards-track documents, and Limited Use and Not Recommended for documents that are off the standards track or have been retired.
sections.plainLanguage: A document climbs three rungs: Proposed Standard, Draft Standard and Internet Standard. Each rung says how much real-world use has been shown. Below the track sit four more labels: Prototype and Experimental for work still in progress, Informational for documents published only for information, and Historic for ones that have been overtaken. A separate statement of requirements says whether implementing a given specification is required, recommended, elective, limited to special cases, or not recommended at all.

sections.title: From Draft to Standard
sections.content:
A standards action, meaning entering a specification into, advancing it within, or removing it from the standards track, must be approved by the IESG. The action is typically initiated by a recommendation to the appropriate IETF Area Director from the group responsible for the specification, usually a Working Group. After completion to the satisfaction of its author and the cognizant Working Group, a document expected to enter or advance is made available as an Internet Draft, and shall remain an Internet Draft for a period permitting useful community review, at least two weeks, before submission to the IESG with a recommendation for action.

The IESG determines whether the specification meets the criteria for the recommended action, and whether an independent technical review is required, commissioning one when necessary. For a specification important enough in terms of its potential impact, the IESG forms an independent technical review and analysis committee to prepare an evaluation, as an objective basis for agreement that the specification is ready. The IESG then communicates its findings to the IETF to permit a final review by the general Internet community. This last-call notification is sent by electronic mail to the IETF mailing list, and for important specifications there is also a presentation or statement during an IETF plenary, where unresolved issues may be raised for final resolution by the IESG. In a timely fashion, but no sooner than two weeks after issuing the last-call notification, the IESG makes its final determination and notifies the IETF by email. After approval and any necessary editorial work, the RFC Editor publishes the specification as an RFC.

A specification shall remain at the Proposed Standard level for at least six months, and at the Draft Standard level for at least four months, or until at least one IETF meeting has occurred, whichever comes later. These intervals are measured from the date of publication of the corresponding RFCs, or, if the action does not result in publication, from the date of IESG approval. A specification may be revised as it advances, and a significant revision may mean it has to accumulate more experience at its current level, or be treated as a new document re-entering the track at the beginning.

When a standards-track specification has not reached Internet Standard but has stayed at the same level for twenty-four months, and every twelve months thereafter, the IESG reviews the viability of the effort, approves termination or continuation, and communicates that decision to the IETF. A new version of an established Standard must progress through the full process as if it were completely new; once it reaches Standard level it usually replaces the previous version, which moves to Historic status, though in some cases both versions may remain as Internet Standards to honour an installed base. As technology matures, the IESG may approve a change of status from Standard to Historic for a superseded specification, using the same last-call and notification procedures as any other standards action.
sections.plainLanguage: A standards action starts with a working group asking its area director for a change, and it normally begins with a public draft that sits for at least two weeks. The IESG then checks the document, may order an independent review, announces a last call for comments, and waits at least two more weeks before deciding. Each rung also has a minimum wait: six months at Proposed Standard, and four months at Draft Standard or until the next IETF meeting, whichever is later. A document that stalls for two years is reviewed to see whether the effort is still alive.

sections.title: Conflict Resolution and Appeals
sections.content:
IETF Working Groups are generally able to reach consensus, which sometimes requires difficult compromises between differing technical solutions. However, there are times when even reasonable and knowledgeable people are unable to agree, and to achieve the goals of openness and fairness such conflicts must be resolved with a process of open review and discussion.

Participants who disagree with Working Group decisions may do so because they believe their own views are not being adequately considered, or because they believe the Working Group made a technical choice that will not work. The first is a difficulty with Working Group process and the latter an assertion of technical error, but the resolution process is the same in both cases.

Participants should first discuss their concerns with the Working Group chair. If that proves unsatisfactory they should raise them with an IESG Area Director or other IESG member, and in most cases the issue will receive consideration by the entire IESG, with the relevant Area Director or the IETF Chair tasked with communicating the results. There are also two opportunities for explicit comment by the wider community: a specification being suggested for advancement may be presented during an IETF plenary, where participants may raise issues or pursue them privately, and specifications to be considered by the IESG are publicly announced to the IETF mailing list with a request for comments. Finally, if a problem persists, the IAB may be asked to adjudicate the dispute.
sections.plainLanguage: Disagreement inside a working group is normal and expected. The RFC sets out where to take it: first the chair, then the area director or the IESG, then the wider IETF through a plenary or a public mailing list announcement. If the problem still stands, the IAB can be asked to settle it. The same route is used whether the objection is about the process or about the technical choice.

sections.title: Intellectual Property Rights and Security
sections.content:
The intellectual property section was completely revised in this revision, in accordance with legal advice, and replaces Sections 5 and 6 of RFC 1310. Its general policy is to benefit the Internet community and the public at large while respecting the legitimate rights of others. The section defines its terms, including trade secrets, contribution, standards track documents, copyrights, ISOC, standards work and Internet community.

On trade secrets, ISOC will not accept, in connection with standards work, any idea, technology, information, document, specification, work or other contribution, whether written or oral, that is a trade secret or otherwise subject to any commitment, understanding or agreement to keep it confidential or otherwise restrict its use or dissemination, and ISOC does not assume any confidentiality obligation with respect to any such contribution. The section then covers rights and permissions, notices and assurances. Assignment of these responsibilities to the IESG is listed among the changes made in this revision, together with the new appeals procedure.

The document's own Security Considerations section says that security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The intellectual property rules were rewritten for this revision on legal advice. The short version is that contributions to standards work must not be trade secrets and must not be subject to a promise of confidentiality, and that the Internet Society takes on no confidentiality obligation for what it receives. The rest of the section covers permissions, notices and assurances. As for security, the document says nothing about it.

messages.label: RECOMMENDATION
messages.note: The group asks for a standards action.

messages.label: INTERNET DRAFT
messages.note: The draft stays public for at least two weeks first.

messages.label: LAST CALL
messages.note: The IESG announces the document to the mailing list and asks for comments.

messages.label: DECISION
messages.note: At least two weeks after the last call, the IESG announces its decision.

messages.label: PUBLICATION
messages.note: After approval and editorial work, the RFC Editor publishes the specification.
